title:
Comment of Nicolette Corbett in Docket(s)/Project(s) P-15423-000
Submission Date: 11/2/2026

documents.name: 152173.txt
documents.text:
Nicolette Corbett, Soldotna, AK.
RE: Opposition to DeepGreen Cook Inlet Subsea-Compute & Infrastructure Hub Project — FERC Project No. P-15423-000

To the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission:

I am submitting this comment in strong opposition to DeepGreen Cook Inlet SPV, LLC's application for a preliminary permit for the proposed DeepGreen Cook Inlet Subsea-Compute & Infrastructure Hub Project.

I am a Yup’ik woman, an Alaska Native, a mother, and a resident of the Kenai Peninsula. I am deeply concerned about the continued push to industrialize Alaska's lands and waters without adequately addressing the long-term consequences for our ecosystems, wildlife, communities, and future generations.

Why in the world are we considering putting an enormous data center UNDER COOK INLET?

According to the federal notice, this proposal includes approximately 330–350 underwater turbines, 66 subsea data center pods, and a 3.5-mile underwater cable system.

Cook Inlet is not an empty body of water waiting to be industrialized.

It is a living ecosystem that supports endangered Cook Inlet beluga whales, salmon, marine mammals, fisheries, and communities whose livelihoods and cultural practices depend on healthy waters.

I have several serious concerns that must be addressed.

First, what are the potential consequences for endangered Cook Inlet beluga whales?

How will hundreds of underwater turbines affect marine mammal movement, underwater noise, prey availability, and habitat? What measures would prevent injury or disturbance? What happens if equipment malfunctions?

Second, what happens to salmon and other fish species?

How will these turbines affect fish migration, juvenile salmon, marine food webs, and commercial, personal-use, and subsistence fisheries?

Third, what happens to the surrounding marine environment when underwater computer servers generate heat?

Where is the independent thermal modeling? What happens during slack tides when water movement slows? How will potential temperature changes affect marine organisms?

Fourth, what happens when something goes wrong?

Cook Inlet is known for extreme tides, powerful currents, sediment movement, ice, and challenging marine conditions. What happens if equipment fails, cables are damaged, or infrastructure breaks apart? Who is responsible for recovering damaged equipment and paying for environmental restoration?

Fifth, who actually benefits from this project?

The application estimates approximately 100 megawatts of electricity generation, primarily intended to power the underwater data center.

Why should Alaska's marine ecosystem bear the environmental risks of generating electricity primarily for private computing operations?

What measurable benefits would Alaska residents receive?

And finally, where is the meaningful consultation with Alaska Native Tribes, fishing communities, and residents who depend on Cook Inlet?

Our waters are not simply industrial real estate.

They sustain our families, our food systems, our economies, and our traditional ways of life.

I recognize that a preliminary permit would not authorize construction. However, granting priority to pursue a future license is still a significant step in advancing this proposal.

I urge FERC to reject this preliminary permit application unless and until the applicant demonstrates that the proposed project is environmentally feasible, that meaningful Tribal and community engagement has occurred, and that the risks to endangered species, fisheries, and marine ecosystems can be adequately evaluated.

We should not be experimenting with hundreds of underwater turbines and computer servers in one of Alaska's most ecologically important marine environments without comprehensive independent scientific review.

Our endangered beluga whales cannot advocate for themselves. Our salmon cannot submit public comments. Our future generations cannot participate in today's decisions.

But we can.

And I am choosing to speak up.

Protect Cook Inlet. Protect our marine mammals. Protect our salmon. Protect our future generations.

Respectfully,

Nikki Corbett

Kenai Peninsula, Alaska
